title: Given an array of `n+1` integers where each integer is in the range `1` to `n`, exactly one number is repeated (possibly multiple times). Find the duplicate without modifying the array if required, and discuss both the Cyclic Sort and Floyd's cycle approaches.
shortTitle: Find the Duplicate Number (Single Repeated Value in 1..n)

s1_definition.profdef: With `n+1` values in range `1..n`, the pigeonhole principle guarantees a duplicate. Cyclic Sort finds it by placing each value `v` at index `v-1`; the moment a value is about to be swapped into a slot that already holds the same value, that value is the duplicate. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare treats the array as a linked list (`next = nums[i]`) and finds the cycle entrance, which is the duplicate, without mutating the array.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has one more loan application than it has application numbers, so by simple counting at least one number was reused. A clerk files each application in its numbered slot, and the first time they find a slot already holding the same application number, that is the reused number.
s1_definition.oneliner: Place each value at its home index; the first time the home already holds that same value, you have found the duplicate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** With `n+1` values in range `1..n`, the pigeonhole principle guarantees a duplicate. Cyclic Sort finds it by placing each value `v` at index `v-1`; the moment a value is about to be swapped into a slot that already holds the same value, that value is the duplicate. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare treats the array as a linked list (`next = nums[i]`) and finds the cycle entrance, which is the duplicate, without mutating the array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has one more loan application than it has application numbers, so by simple counting at least one number was reused. A clerk files each application in its numbered slot, and the first time they find a slot already holding the same application number, that is the reused number.

**One line to remember:** Place each value at its home index; the first time the home already holds that same value, you have found the duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
The Cyclic Sort approach runs the placement loop, but instead of finishing the sort it returns early: when `nums[i] != i+1` and `nums[i] == nums[nums[i]-1]`, the value `nums[i]` already lives at its home and yet appears again here, so it is the duplicate. This mutates the array and is O(n) time, O(1) space.

When mutation is forbidden, Floyd's algorithm is the senior answer. Interpret each value as a pointer: from index `i` you jump to index `nums[i]`. Because `n+1` values map into `1..n`, this functional graph must contain a cycle, and the cycle's entry point is the duplicate. A slow pointer advances one step and a fast pointer two steps until they meet inside the cycle, then a second walk from the start and from the meeting point at equal speed meets exactly at the duplicate. For example `int[] apps = {1,3,4,2,2};` has fast and slow meet, and the entry walk lands on 2.

A senior-level nuance is the trade-off: Cyclic Sort is simpler to explain and reason about but destroys the input; Floyd's is read-only and uses O(1) space but is harder to justify on the spot. Binary search on the value range counting how many elements are less than or equal to mid is a third O(n log n) read-only option. I pick Floyd's when the array must stay intact and Cyclic Sort when mutation is acceptable and clarity matters.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India batches loan applications and assigns each a number from 1 to n, but a feed glitch occasionally duplicates one application number across n+1 records. Before approval the system must flag the reused number so the duplicate record can be purged, and in the audited pipeline the original array of record numbers must not be mutated because downstream checks re-read it. This is exactly the find-the-duplicate problem, and because mutation is forbidden here we use Floyd's cycle detection, treating each record number as a pointer to the next index.

The code contains a `LoanDuplicateDetector` with a mutating `findDuplicateCyclic(int[])` and a read-only `findDuplicateFloyd(int[])`, plus a demo comparing both on the same feed.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: `feed = {1,3,4,2,2}`, n=4.

Step 1 (Floyd): slow and fast both start at `nums[0]=1`. slow becomes `nums[1]=3`; fast becomes `nums[nums[1]]=nums[3]=2`. Next, slow becomes `nums[3]=2`; fast becomes `nums[nums[2]]=nums[4]=2`. slow equals fast at 2, so they meet in the cycle.

Step 2 (Floyd): reset slow to `nums[0]=1`. slow and fast advance one step each: slow becomes `nums[1]=3`, fast becomes `nums[2]=4`; they differ. slow becomes `nums[3]=2`, fast becomes `nums[4]=2`; equal, so the entry is 2, the duplicate.

Step 3 (Cyclic on a clone): placement proceeds until a value finds its home already occupied by the same value; that collision happens at value 2, which is returned immediately.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Loan application numbers: [1, 3, 4, 2, 2]
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Duplicate via Floyd (array untouched): 2
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Duplicate via Cyclic Sort: 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: feed = [1,3,4,2,2]  (n+1 values in 1..n)
    │
    ├─ READ-ONLY (Floyd)                 ├─ MUTATING (Cyclic)
    │  slow/fast meet at 2               │  place until home occupied
    │  entry walk → 2                    │  collision at value 2
    ▼                                    ▼
  duplicate = 2                        duplicate = 2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the single duplicate in an array of n plus one values drawn from the range one to n starts with the pigeonhole principle: more values than available numbers guarantees a repeat. If I am allowed to mutate the array I use Cyclic Sort, placing each value at the index equal to the value minus one, and the instant I try to send a value home only to find the same value already sitting there, that value is the duplicate. This is linear time and constant space and is the easiest version to explain.

When the array must stay intact, which is common in audited banking pipelines, I switch to Floyd's tortoise-and-hare. I treat each value as a pointer from index i to index nums at i, which turns the array into a functional graph that must contain a cycle because n plus one slots map into n targets. A slow pointer and a fast pointer meet inside the cycle, and then a second walk from the start and from the meeting point at equal speed meets exactly at the cycle entrance, which is the duplicate. This is also linear time and constant space but never writes to the array.

In my work at the National Bank of India this guarded the loan application feed, where a glitch occasionally reused one application number across the records. Downstream approval steps re-read the original record array, so mutation was not acceptable, and I used Floyd's cycle detection to name the reused number without touching the input. I always present both approaches in an interview and state the deciding factor plainly: Cyclic Sort when mutation is fine and clarity matters, Floyd's when the array is read-only.
